docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
After International Space Station (ISS) missions, crew balance with eyes closed on a sway-referenced support had a mean equilibrium score of 74.9 before flight, and the NASA recovery model estimates 13.2 at landing (n = 37, Wood et al. 2015). In a separate NASA study of 11 first-time astronauts tested 2–5 h after Space Shuttle landing, 20 of 22 eyes-closed trials with prescribed head movements ended in a fall (Jain et al. 2010). NASA lists the Risk of Altered Sensorimotor/Vestibular Function Impacting Critical Mission Tasks among the risks of human spaceflight.

The Gravity-Transition Readiness Model addresses the first task after landing: leaving the vehicle. It converts a standing-balance test into one of four results, GO, CAUTION, NO-GO or CANNOT ASSESS, names the rule that produced it and states the next action. When the result is not GO, it estimates the retest time from the published NASA crew recovery model.

The model is deterministic. The thresholds combine published values, reference data from healthy adults and stated design choices, each documented with its source, and every result can be traced to a numbered rule. No model is trained, because no public dataset known to us labels individuals as fit or unfit to leave a vehicle.

docs.title: What the application provides
docs.text:
• An interactive model. The user sets the inputs of a balance test, and the result, the rule applied and the recommended action update immediately.
  • Explicit safety rules. Seven numbered rules, applied in a fixed order. A fall always yields NO-GO, an invalid recording yields CANNOT ASSESS, and overall GO requires two GO sessions at least 2 h apart.
  • A retest estimate. The time at which typical NASA crew recovery brings every condition to its GO threshold, with a range from the published confidence limits.
  • A comparison with typical NASA crew. Each recorded session is placed on the NASA recovery curve of each condition.
  • Traceable data. Every cited value is listed with its source and page, and every simulated result is labelled as simulated.

The output supports the crew surgeon and does not constitute clearance.

docs.title: About
docs.text: The Gravity-Transition Readiness Model was developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, in response to the challenge Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Most health-monitoring tools display vital signs. This prototype converts a measurement into a decision at a moment that NASA documents as hazardous: leaving the vehicle after landing. It addresses one part of crew health monitoring, sensorimotor readiness, and is designed so that further modules can be added on the same principle of comparison with the crew member's own preflight values. The Additional crew data tab already presents NASA OSDR crew blood panels in this form, as context.

docs.title: Intended use
docs.text: The application supports the crew surgeon. It does not constitute clearance, and its thresholds are provisional and have not been validated for egress. It is a prototype for research and demonstration and is not a medical device.

docs.title: Code and reproducibility
docs.text: The source code, tests, demonstration data and validation report are available in the repository. Every value reported on this site can be reproduced with the scripts described in the repository README.

docs.title: Use of AI
docs.text: AI was used to assist in collecting literature, writing code and refining language.

docs.title: Human Balance Evaluation Database
docs.text:
The Human Balance Evaluation Database (Santos and Duarte 2016, PhysioNet) contains force-plate recordings of 163 adults: 1,930 trials of 60 s at 100 Hz, in the four conditions used here. It provides the baselines, the test–retest margins and the population floors. Three participants form the demonstration set:

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Baseline The crew member's preflight equilibrium score in a condition, the median of three trials. CANNOT ASSESS The result when a recording is invalid or session times are missing or out of order. Never GO. CAUTION The result when a score lies between the 75% line and the GO threshold, below the population floor, or when a single GO session awaits confirmation. Centre of mass The point at which the body's mass can be considered concentrated. Its sway is used to compute the equilibrium score. Centre of pressure The point of application of the ground-reaction force under the feet, recorded by the force plate. Confirmatory session A second GO session, at least 2 h after the first, required for an overall GO. Equilibrium score (EQ) 100 × (1 − θ / 12.5°), where θ is the peak-to-peak anterior–posterior sway angle over 20 s. A score of 100 indicates no sway. Force plate A platform that measures the forces and moments applied by a person standing on it. GO The result when two consecutive recorded sessions at least 2 h apart are GO in every condition. The egress decision rests with the crew surgeon. GO threshold The ratio to baseline a score must reach for GO: the larger of 0.75 × the test–retest margin and the population floor divided by the baseline. NO-GO The result after a fall or a score below 75% of baseline. Population floor The 5th percentile of healthy reference scores in the same condition and age group. Ratio to baseline The session score divided by the baseline in the same condition. Recovery time constant (τ) The time in which the remaining deficit falls to about 37% of its value, in the NASA crew recovery model. Sensory Organization Test NASA's force-plate balance test, with six conditions that alter visual and somatosensory information. Sway-referenced support A platform that tilts with the person's sway, so that ankle position gives little information about body orientation. Test–retest margin (q95) The 95th percentile of the ratio between two measurements of the same person when no true change has occurred.

docs.title: Technical documentation
docs.text:
This section describes how a balance recording becomes a decision and a retest estimate. Each page states the method, the source of every value and the assumption it rests on.

Page Content Measurement and score Test protocol, centre-of-mass estimation and the equilibrium score Decision rules The seven rules, the GO threshold and the two-session requirement Retest estimate The NASA crew recovery model applied to an individual measurement Pharmacological scenario Promethazine concentration and its effect on the retest estimate Validation Calibration against NASA crew data, healthy retest and automated tests Assumptions and limitations What the model assumes and what it does not establish

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
1. Status comes only from a measured test. The recovery forecast estimates when to retest and never yields GO.
  2. Each person is compared with their own baseline. Scores are expressed as a ratio to the crew member's preflight score in the same condition, never across conditions.
  3. Rules are explicit and ordered. Every result names the rule that produced it.
  4. Uncertainty favours a retest. Test–retest variability is allowed for before GO is returned, and an overall GO requires two sessions.
  5. Nothing is trained. No public dataset known to us labels individuals as fit or unfit to leave a vehicle. The thresholds combine published values, healthy reference data and stated design choices, such as the 2-h interval between sessions.

The application is written in Python. The decision engine (readiness/decision.py), the forecast (readiness/forecast.py), the signal processing (readiness/signals.py) and the pharmacological model (readiness/medicine.py) are separate modules, and the interface (app.py, Streamlit) only displays their output.

docs.title: Rules within a condition
docs.text:
For each condition, the rules are applied in numerical order, and the first rule that applies sets the result.

Rule Condition Result 1 Any trial invalid, fewer than three trials, or baseline missing or invalid CANNOT ASSESS 2 Any trial ended in a fall or was stopped NO-GO 3 \(r_c < 0.75\) NO-GO 4 Session score below the healthy population floor \(P5_c\) CAUTION and referral 5 \(r_c \ge q_c\) (GO threshold) GO 6 Any other score CAUTION 7 Overall result and two-session requirement see below

Rule 3: the 75% line. Jain et al. (2010) regarded a decrement of less than 25% from a crew member's own preflight score as recovery. A score below 75% of baseline therefore yields NO-GO.

Rule 4: the population floor. Jain et al. (2010) regarded a score below the 5th percentile of normative data as clinically abnormal. The floor \(P5_c\) is the 5th percentile of reference scores in the same condition and age group, from HBEDB participants without a reported disability, excluding reported labyrinthitis (see Validation). A crew member whose score is below the floor is referred to the crew surgeon, even when the score is close to their own baseline.

docs.title: The GO threshold
docs.text:
A single test is noisy. A score just above 75% of baseline may come from a true score below it. The GO threshold therefore keeps the score at or above 75% of baseline after allowance for test–retest variability, and at or above the population floor:

\[ q_c = \max\!\left(0.75\,q_{95,c},\; \frac{P5_c}{b_c}\right) \]

The margin \(q_{95,c}\) is the 95th percentile of the ratio between the median of three retest trials and the median of three baseline trials when no true change has occurred. It is the larger of two estimates:

  • From data. Residuals of healthy HBEDB participants, by condition, age group and baseline tertile, resampled 200,000 times.
  • From the literature. The minimal detectable change of the head-shake Sensory Organization Test reported by Pang et al. (2011), 2.7 (younger) and 3.6 (older) points on the firm conditions and 16.2 and 22.7 points on the foam conditions. Each value, reported for a five-trial mean, is converted to a per-trial standard deviation, \(\mathrm{MDC}\sqrt{5}/(1.96\sqrt{2})\), and three-trial medians are simulated 100,000 times at each baseline level with independent, normally distributed errors.

The literature margin is a transfer. Pang et al. measured five-trial means with head movements on firm and sway-referenced surfaces and divided age groups at 50 years. Here it is applied to three-trial medians with the head still, including foam, with the HBEDB age groups divided at 60 years. Taking the larger of the two margins is the cautious choice.

If \(q_c \ge 1\), the GO threshold lies at or above baseline. A condition whose score is still below such a threshold cannot reach it under the recovery model, and no retest time is estimated. A condition already at or above its threshold needs no recovery.

Example. For participant A on foam with eyes closed, \(b = 84.7\), \(q_{95} = 1.267\) and \(P5 = 77.1\), so \(q = \max(0.950, 0.910) = 0.950\). A score must reach 95% of baseline for GO.

docs.title: Published values and design choices
docs.text: Quantity Origin 75% line Published: working definition of recovery (Jain et al. 2010) 5th-percentile floor Published criterion (Jain et al. 2010), computed from HBEDB reference data Test–retest margin Computed from HBEDB data and from published values (Pang et al. 2011), with the transfer assumptions above Two sessions, at least 2 h apart Design choice Recovery model Published (Wood et al. 2015, Table III)

docs.title: Overall result (rule 7)
docs.text:
• The overall result is that of the least favourable condition, in the order CANNOT ASSESS, NO-GO, CAUTION, GO.
  • A test with a condition that was not measured cannot yield GO and is limited to CAUTION.
  • Overall GO requires two consecutive GO tests in separate recorded sessions at least 2 h apart. A single GO session gives CAUTION with a request for a confirmatory session. Session times must be strictly increasing, otherwise the result is CANNOT ASSESS.
  • The retest estimate never yields GO. Only a measured session can.

docs.title: Recommended actions
docs.text: Situation Recommended action NO-GO Do not leave the vehicle unassisted. Retest at the estimated time, or refer to the crew surgeon if no time can be estimated or a fall occurred CAUTION after one GO session A confirmatory test in a separate session at least 2 h later CAUTION for any other reason Retest at the estimated time, or refer to the crew surgeon CANNOT ASSESS Repeat the test with valid recordings, or correct the session times GO No further testing is required under the decision rules. The egress decision rests with the crew surgeon

docs.title: Retest estimate
docs.text: When a session is CAUTION or NO-GO after a landing, the application estimates when every condition is expected to reach its GO threshold. The estimate tells the crew surgeon when a retest is worthwhile. It never yields GO.

docs.title: NASA crew recovery model
docs.text:
Wood et al. (2015) fitted an exponential recovery model to Sensory Organization Test scores of 37 ISS crew members after landing. Expressed as a ratio to the preflight mean, the typical recovery in condition \(c\) is

\[ r_c(t) = 1 - D_c\, e^{-t/\tau_c}, \qquad D_c = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{EQ}_{c}(0)}{\mathrm{EQ}_{c,\text{pre}}} \]

where \(t\) is the time after landing in hours, \(\mathrm{EQ}_c(0)\) the fitted landing-day score and \(\tau_c\) the recovery time constant.

Condition NASA analogue Preflight mean Landing day (95% limits) \(\tau\), h (95% limits) \(D\) Firm floor, eyes open SOT 1 94.3 90.0 (±2.2) 116.1 (±86.6) 0.046 Firm floor, eyes closed SOT 2 89.9 82.6 (±3.9) 99.4 (±74.6) 0.081 Foam, eyes open SOT 4 87.9 68.2 (±8.3) 44.6 (±25.6) 0.224 Foam, eyes closed SOT 5 74.9 13.2 (±21.1) 19.4 (±10.7) 0.824

Source: Wood et al. (2015), Table III, p. A49. The mapping of the conditions used here to the NASA conditions is stated in Measurement and score.

docs.title: Applying the model to an individual
docs.text:
The typical recovery rate is applied to the deficit measured in the crew member. A session at time \(t_m\) with ratio \(r_m\) fixes the individual deficit

\[ D_i = (1 - r_m)\, e^{t_m/\tau_c} \]

so that the curve passes through the measurement. The time after the session at which the curve reaches the GO threshold \(q_c\) is

\[ \Delta t_c = \tau_c \ln\!\left(\frac{1 - r_m}{1 - q_c}\right) \]

The retest estimate is the largest \(\Delta t_c\) across the four conditions, because every condition must be GO. The range is obtained by repeating the calculation with the lower and upper 95% limits of \(\tau_c\). It describes the uncertainty of the published crew model, not a 95% interval for the individual.

If \(q_c \ge 1\) in a condition whose score is still below its threshold, the threshold cannot be reached under the model, and no time is given. A condition that is already at or above its threshold needs no recovery and is excluded from the estimate, unless a planned dose is predicted to lower it.

A retest time later than 240 h after landing, with or without a planned dose, is labelled in the application as an extrapolation of the recovery model.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Participant A, 6 h after a simulated landing:

Condition \(r_m\) \(q\) \(\tau\), h \(\Delta t\), h (range) Firm floor, eyes open 0.957 0.975 116.1 62.9 (16.0–109.9) Firm floor, eyes closed 0.924 0.950 99.4 41.2 (10.3–72.2) Foam, eyes open 0.804 0.946 44.6 57.6 (24.5–90.7) Foam, eyes closed 0.395 0.950 19.4 48.5 (21.7–75.2)

Foam with eyes closed causes the NO-GO, but firm floor with eyes open reaches its threshold last. The application reports a retest in approximately 63 h (≈69 h after landing), with a range of 25–110 h, the largest lower and upper values across conditions.

docs.title: Comparison with typical NASA crew
docs.text: After a landing, the application also plots each recorded session on the curve \(r_c(t)\) of each condition and reports the difference from the typical crew member at the latest session, in percentage points of baseline. With several sessions, the points show whether the crew member recovers faster or slower than the typical crew member. This comparison is descriptive and does not enter the decision.

docs.title: Assumptions and limitations
docs.text: The application supports the decision of a crew surgeon and is not a clearance authority. Every threshold is a provisional decision assumption informed by NASA working definitions, not a validated egress boundary.

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text: Assumption Basis A1 Firm floor with eyes open and closed corresponds to Sensory Organization Test conditions 1 and 2 in sensory content. Foam approximates conditions 4 and 5. Jain et al. (2010); Bermúdez Rey et al. (2016) A2 The typical recovery rate of ISS crew applies to the measured deficit of an individual. Wood et al. (2015) describe the median crew member A3 The 25% decrement, the 5th-percentile floor, the test–retest margin and the 2-h two-session rule are suitable decision thresholds. Jain et al. (2010); HBEDB; Pang et al. (2011) A4 Promethazine concentration is proportional to dose, and its effect is linear in concentration. Gandia et al. (2006), 50 mg study A5 The link between promethazine and balance follows the vestibular-ageing equivalence described in Pharmacological scenario. Diaz-Artiles et al. (2017); Bermúdez Rey et al. (2016) A6 The zero-point-to-zero-point centre-of-mass estimator gives scores comparable with the NASA estimator. Calibration on the firm conditions A7 Recovery after landing on the Moon (0.17 g) or Mars (0.38 g) follows the Earth-return data. Not characterised (transfer assumption) A8 The test is administered with a spotter or a safety harness. Test design A9 Two GO sessions at least 2 h apart are sufficient confirmation. Design choice

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The HBEDB participants are not astronauts, and each was recorded in a single session, so day-to-day test–retest variability is not measured. Their reference scores serve as preflight proxies.
  • No public dataset labels individuals as fit or unfit to leave a vehicle, so the thresholds cannot be validated against outcomes.
  • Post-landing sessions in the demonstration are simulated by scaling a participant's own trials onto the typical NASA crew recovery curve, and they are labelled as simulated.
  • The benefit of the two-session rule assumes independent retest errors. Learning effects reduce it.
  • Under literature-level test–retest variability, older adults rarely reach GO on foam. This is a deliberate safety trade-off.
  • The single-exponential model of Wood et al. (2015) does not represent the slower recovery phase over the following weeks. Sessions can be recorded up to 240 h after landing. A retest time later than 240 h is labelled in the application as an extrapolation of the recovery model.
  • The healthy reference group is a general adult population (participants without a reported disability, excluding labyrinthitis) rather than a screened astronaut population.
  • A reliable preflight baseline requires familiarisation sessions. The protocol is not specified here.
  • Tolerability of foam testing on landing day is unresolved. Jain et al. (2010) report that it was abandoned after one Shuttle crew reported concern that it disrupted their postflight recovery.
  • The literature test–retest margin is transferred from a different protocol and age split (Pang et al. 2011), as described in Decision rules.
  • The pharmacological scenario is unvalidated and adjusts only the retest estimate.

docs.title: Test protocol
docs.text:
The crew member stands still on a force plate for three 20-s trials in each of four sensory conditions.

Condition Sensory information available NASA analogue Firm floor, eyes open Vision, vestibular, somatosensory Sensory Organization Test condition 1 Firm floor, eyes closed Vestibular, somatosensory Condition 2 Foam, eyes open Vision, vestibular, reduced somatosensory Condition 4 (approximation) Foam, eyes closed Vestibular, reduced somatosensory Condition 5 (approximation)

Condition 5, with eyes closed on a sway-referenced support, is the condition most affected after spaceflight because the crew member must rely on the vestibular system. NASA uses a sway-referenced platform. This prototype uses foam, which Jain et al. (2010) proposed as a simpler substitute while noting that the two are not strictly equivalent. They also report that foam testing was tried with one Shuttle crew on landing day and abandoned after the crew reported concern that it disrupted their postflight recovery. Tolerability of the test on landing day is therefore unresolved.

The test challenges balance in crew members who may fall. It is administered with a spotter or a safety harness, and a fall is recorded as a trial outcome.

docs.title: From force plate to centre of mass
docs.text:
The force plate records the centre of pressure and the horizontal ground-reaction force at 100 Hz. The centre of mass is estimated by zero-point-to-zero-point double integration (Zatsiorsky and King 1998). When the horizontal force is zero, the centre of mass lies directly above the centre of pressure. Between consecutive zero crossings, the horizontal acceleration \(a = -F_x / m\) is integrated twice, with the initial velocity chosen so that the centre of mass coincides with the centre of pressure at both crossings.

This estimator is an adaptation. Wood et al. (2015) estimated the centre of mass by low-pass filtering the centre of pressure (second-order Butterworth, 0.85 Hz). The equilibrium-score formula is the same, but the complete NASA measurement pipeline is not reproduced.

The first complete 20-s window of each trial is used. A window is accepted only if at least 99% of its samples are valid and the sway exceeds the instrument noise floor.

docs.title: Equilibrium score
docs.text:
The equilibrium score converts the peak-to-peak anterior–posterior sway of the centre of mass over 20 s into a sway angle relative to the height of the centre of mass, taken as 0.55 of body height \(H\):

\[ \theta = \arctan\!\left(\frac{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}{0.55\,H}\right), \qquad \mathrm{EQ} = 100\left(1 - \frac{\theta}{12.5^\circ}\right) \]

where 12.5° is the limit of stability. A score of 100 indicates no sway. The score is multiplied by the fraction of the trial completed and is not allowed to fall below 0. A fall yields NO-GO whatever the score (rule 2).

Worked example. For the first baseline trial of participant A on foam with eyes closed (HBEDB trial BDS01402), the peak-to-peak sway is 2.87 cm and the body height 156 cm:

\[ \theta = \arctan\!\left(\frac{2.87}{0.55 \times 156}\right) = 1.91^\circ, \qquad \mathrm{EQ} = 100\left(1 - \frac{1.91}{12.5}\right) = 84.7 \]

The application reproduces this computation in the tab From force plate to score.

A recorded baseline trial, its peak-to-peak sway and the resulting equilibrium score.

docs.title: Score relative to baseline
docs.text:
For each condition \(c\), the session score is the median of the three trial scores, and the decision uses its ratio to the crew member's preflight baseline in the same condition:

\[ r_c = \frac{\operatorname{median}(\mathrm{EQ}_{c,1}, \mathrm{EQ}_{c,2}, \mathrm{EQ}_{c,3})}{b_c} \]

The baseline \(b_c\) is the median of the three preflight trials. A score is never compared with a baseline from a different condition.

Balance scores improve with repeated testing. Jain et al. (2010) excluded the first two preflight sessions for this reason, and Wood et al. (2015) used the last of two preflight sessions. A baseline taken without familiarisation underestimates true performance and inflates later ratios. The familiarisation protocol is not specified in this prototype, and the single-session HBEDB recordings used as preflight proxies cannot establish it.

docs.title: Pharmacological scenario
docs.text:
Promethazine is used to treat space motion sickness. It is also sedating and may impair balance. The application lets the crew surgeon enter a planned dose and see how it could shift the retest estimate.

Unvalidated scenario

The effect of promethazine on balance after landing has not been measured. The scenario adjusts only the retest estimate. A dose is entered as planned at or after the test, so it never changes a test result.

docs.title: Concentration
docs.text:
Plasma concentration follows a one-compartment model with first-order absorption:

\[ C(t) = A\left(e^{-k_e t} - e^{-k_a t}\right), \qquad k_e = \frac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}} \]

with \(k_a\) solved from the time of peak concentration and \(A\) scaled so that the peak equals the published maximum. Concentration is assumed to be proportional to dose.

Route (50 mg) \(t_{1/2}\), h \(t_{\max}\), h \(C_{\max}\), µg/L Oral 15.6 2.9 22.5 Intramuscular 17.8 2.0 52.4

Source: Gandia et al. (2006), Table II (ambulatory phase of a bed-rest study). Available doses are 12.5, 25 and 50 mg.

docs.title: Effect on balance
docs.text:
Concentration is expressed relative to the extrapolated peak of a 25 mg oral dose (11.25 µg/L). Diaz-Artiles et al. (2017) reported that 25 mg oral promethazine raised the roll-tilt perception threshold by 31%, and Bermúdez Rey et al. (2016) reported a rise of 32% per decade of age in the same threshold. A 25 mg oral peak is therefore treated as equivalent to 0.97 of a decade of vestibular ageing, and the ratio decrement is

\[ \delta_c(t) = 0.97\, C_{\text{rel}}(t)\, \frac{b'_c}{b_c} \]

where \(b'_c\) is the decline in equilibrium score per decade of age estimated from HBEDB. The effect is applied only in conditions where this age slope is established (foam with eyes open). The drug never raises a score.

docs.title: Warnings shown with a dose
docs.text:
• Orthostatic risk. In a NASA study of 8 healthy participants given intravenous promethazine, all 8 became presyncopal on tilt testing, compared with 3 of 8 without the drug (Shi et al. 2011). Stand only with assistance.
  • Absorption in flight. A lower and later peak concentration has been reported in flight (Boyd et al. 2009). Only the direction of this difference is known, and it is not modelled.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: The values below are produced by scripts/validate.py from the full Human Balance Evaluation Database (163 adults, 1,930 trials) and are reported in out/VALIDATION.md in the repository.

docs.title: Reference cohort
docs.text: In this model, the healthy reference group comprises HBEDB participants without a reported disability, excluding those reporting labyrinthitis. Other illnesses and medication are not excluded: of the 140 participants, 86 report an illness and 89 a medication. The group therefore represents a general adult population rather than a screened astronaut population. Its floors and margins are provisional proxies for crew values, and whether they are more or less conservative than crew-specific values has not been established.

docs.title: Calibration against NASA crew preflight scores
docs.text:
Healthy adults aged 25–55 years (n = 43), scored with the method described in Measurement and score, compared with the preflight means of 37 ISS crew members (Wood et al. 2015, Table III). The tolerance for the firm conditions, 5 points, was set before the comparison.

Condition NASA analogue This model (median) NASA preflight (mean) Difference Firm floor, eyes open SOT 1 94.1 94.3 −0.2 Firm floor, eyes closed SOT 2 92.9 89.9 +3.0 Foam, eyes open SOT 4 86.9 87.9 −1.0 Foam, eyes closed SOT 5 85.8 74.9 +10.9

The firm conditions are within tolerance. On foam with eyes closed, the healthy median is 10.9 points above the NASA mean. The cohorts, estimators and support surfaces differ (foam here, a sway-referenced platform at NASA), so this is an observed difference between protocols rather than a measured effect of the surface. Agreement on the firm conditions does not establish equivalence with the NASA method.

docs.title: Healthy retest
docs.text:
The thresholds were derived from one half of the healthy participants and applied to the other half (two-fold cross-validation by participant). The baseline was the first 20-s window of each trial and the retest the second window of the same trials, so no true change occurred. A single test was scored, without the two-session rule.

Group n GO CAUTION NO-GO All 140 42.9% 56.4% 0.7% Younger 82 72.0% 26.8% 1.2% Older 58 1.7% 98.3% 0.0%

Healthy participants are often held at CAUTION, particularly older participants on foam, where test–retest variability is large. The rules favour a retest over a false clearance.

docs.title: Structural check
docs.text: When every retest trial is set to 74% of the participant's own baseline trials, the ratio is 0.74 in every condition, and the 75% rule returned NO-GO in all four conditions for 140 of 140 participants. This confirms that the rule operates as specified. It is not evidence of safety.

docs.title: Automated tests
docs.text:
The test suite (196 tests on 15 November 2026) checks:

  • every rule against an independent statement of the arithmetic, on 200,000 random inputs including invalid ones,
  • the exact thresholds and malformed inputs,
  • the two-session rules and session ordering,
  • the retest and pharmacological solvers against a dense brute-force search,
  • the real-data values reported on this page,
  • the application itself, in which every example reproduces the result of the decision engine, and randomly set inputs give the engine's result.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
The thresholds are provisional. The following data would allow them to be tested:

  1. Repeated sessions in healthy adults, to measure day-to-day test–retest variability, which the single-session HBEDB recordings do not provide.
  2. Foam and sway-referenced testing in the same participants, to quantify the transfer between the two protocols.
  3. Post-landing crew data with observed egress performance, to set the thresholds against a functional outcome.

docs.title: How to use the app
docs.text:
Open the app in any modern browser. No installation or sign-in is needed. The model runs entirely in the browser, so the first visit takes about 20–40 s to load and later visits are faster.

The application is an interactive model. The inputs of a balance test are set on the left of the page, and the model output on the right updates immediately. No button needs to be pressed to obtain a result.

docs.title: Running it locally
docs.text:
The application can also be run on a local machine with Python 3.11 or later.

git clone https://github.com/vishram0905/gravity-readiness.git
cd gravity-readiness
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv/bin/streamlit run app.py

The application opens in the browser at http://localhost:8501. The demonstration data of three participants are included in the repository, so no download is needed.

docs.title: Page layout
docs.text:
The page six hours after a simulated landing. Left: test inputs. Right: the result card, the chart of each sensory condition against its thresholds, the rule-by-rule table and the numbered decision rules.

From top to bottom, the page contains:

Section Content Header The question addressed, the measurement and the decision, in three short paragraphs Test inputs (left) Example list, crew member baseline, time after landing, equilibrium score and trial outcome for each condition, session history Model output (right) Result card with the rule applied and the recommended action, the NASA data used, the condition chart, the rule table and the decision rules Estimated retest time Shown after a landing when the result is CAUTION or NO-GO Recovery compared with typical NASA crew Shown after a landing. Each session placed on the NASA recovery curve of each condition Tabs From force plate to score · Pharmacological scenario · NASA data and limitations · Additional crew data

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Open Load an example and select A · younger adult · 6 h after landing. The result is NO-GO, because the score on foam with eyes closed is below 75% of baseline. The card recommends a retest in approximately 63 h.
  2. Drag the slider for Foam, eyes closed to the right. The marker on the chart moves, and when the score passes the 75% line the result changes to CAUTION. The other three conditions are still below their GO thresholds at 6 h, so the rule table shows which condition now determines the result.
  3. Set any trial outcome to fall. The result is NO-GO under rule 2, whatever the score.
  4. Select A · younger adult · 71 h after landing, confirmatory session. Two recorded GO sessions give GO, and the egress decision rests with the crew surgeon.

A worked session follows one crew member from landing to GO. Inputs and outputs describes every control and every element of the output.

Simulated post-landing sessions

The participants are healthy adults from the Human Balance Evaluation Database, not astronauts. Post-landing sessions are simulated by scaling each participant's own recorded trials onto the typical NASA crew recovery curve, and the result card labels them SIMULATED EXAMPLE.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
The input column. Control Description Load an example Fills every control with a recorded or simulated test and resets the pharmacological scenario to no dose. The examples are listed below. Crew member baseline Three option buttons. Preflight baseline and age group. The reference scores of three HBEDB participants serve as preflight proxies. Changing the crew member clears the session history. After landing Off for a baseline-day test. On for a test after landing, which enables the time control, the retest estimate and the comparison with NASA crew. Hours after landing 0.5–240 h in steps of 0.5 h. Set scores to typical NASA crew recovery at this time Replaces the scores with the participant's own trial spread placed on the typical NASA recovery curve at the chosen time. Falls and invalid recordings are kept. Equilibrium score per condition One slider per sensory condition (0–100, step 0.1). The label gives the participant's baseline. Enter the three trials separately Replaces each slider with three trial scores. The decision uses their median. Trial outcome completed, fall or invalid recording, for each condition. Record this session Stores the current session with its trial scores, outcomes, time and source, and advances the time by 2 h. Available after a landing, up to 240 h. Clear sessions Removes every recorded session.

Further controls in the tabs:

Control Description Planned dose (mg) Pharmacological scenario tab: 0, 12.5, 25 or 50 mg of promethazine. 0 switches the scenario off. Available only after a landing, when every condition has a valid recording and no fall has occurred. Route Oral or intramuscular. Dose time 0–48 h after the current session, in steps of 0.5 h. Condition From force plate to score tab: the sensory condition whose recorded baseline trial is shown. Analyte Additional crew data tab: one of seven blood analytes.

docs.title: Result card
docs.text:
The card gives the status, the rule applied and the recommended action.

Status Meaning GO Two consecutive GO sessions at least 2 h apart. The egress decision rests with the crew surgeon. CAUTION A single GO session awaiting confirmation, a score between the 75% line and the GO threshold, or a score below the healthy population floor. NO-GO A fall, or a score below 75% of baseline. Do not leave the vehicle unassisted. CANNOT ASSESS An invalid recording, or session times that are missing or out of order.

Each status is shown by word and symbol as well as colour. A tag gives the source of the values: HBEDB RECORDING, SIMULATED EXAMPLE, SIMULATED: TYPICAL NASA RECOVERY or USER-ENTERED VALUES.

docs.title: NASA data in this result
docs.text: A line under the card lists the NASA data that entered the result: the 25% NO-GO criterion (Jain et al. 2010), the equilibrium-score formula of the NASA Sensory Organization Test, the typical ISS crew member at the same time after landing and, where shown, the retest time (Wood et al. 2015).

docs.title: Condition chart
docs.text: Element Meaning Red band Below 75% of baseline (NO-GO, rule 3) Amber band CAUTION band Green band and solid green line At or above the GO threshold (rule 5) Dotted brown line Healthy population floor (rule 4) Diamond / cross Participant's score / a fall Open blue circle Typical ISS crew member at the same time after landing

docs.title: Rule table
docs.text: For each condition, the table shows the score as a percentage of baseline, whether each of rules 1–5 is met, and the resulting status with the rule that produced it. Rules are applied in numerical order, and the first that applies sets the result. The numbered rules are listed under the table, with the applied rule marked.

docs.title: Estimated retest time
docs.text: Shown after a landing when every condition has a valid recording, no fall has occurred and the session is not GO. It is also shown for a GO session when a planned dose is predicted to lower a score below its GO threshold. It is not shown for a GO session awaiting confirmation without a dose, after a fall, or when the result is CANNOT ASSESS, including session times out of order. The chart shows the recovery curve of the condition that reaches its GO threshold last, the estimated retest time and its range. Conditions already at or above their GO threshold need no recovery. When the GO threshold of a condition still below it cannot be reached, no time is shown and the card refers the crew member to the crew surgeon. A retest time later than 240 h after landing is labelled as an extrapolation.

docs.title: Recovery compared with typical NASA crew
docs.text: Shown after a landing. Four panels, one per condition, place the recorded sessions (filled points) and the current session (open point) on the NASA recovery curve. Invalid recordings and a session timed before the last recorded session are not plotted.

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text: Tab Content From force plate to score A recorded baseline trial of the participant and the step-by-step computation of its equilibrium score Pharmacological scenario A planned promethazine dose and its effect on the retest estimate, with warnings NASA data and limitations Sources, protocol and transfer assumptions, validation and safeguards Additional crew data (context) NASA OSDR Inspiration4 crew blood panels relative to each crew member's preflight mean. Context only

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Example Result Rule A · younger adult · 6 h after landing NO-GO, retest in approximately 63 h 3 A · younger adult · 69 h after landing, first GO CAUTION, confirmatory session required 7 A · younger adult · 71 h after landing, confirmatory session GO 7 A · younger adult · baseline day, simulated fall NO-GO 2 A · younger adult · baseline day, no landing CAUTION, confirmatory session required 7 B · older adult · 6 h after landing NO-GO, no retest estimate 3 B · older adult · 240 h after landing, GO not reached CAUTION 6 B · older adult · baseline day, simulated fall NO-GO 2 B · older adult · baseline day, no landing CAUTION 6 C · low baseline balance · 6 h after landing NO-GO, no retest estimate 3 C · low baseline balance · 240 h after landing, GO not reached CAUTION 4 C · low baseline balance · baseline day, simulated fall NO-GO 2 C · low baseline balance · baseline day, no landing CAUTION 4

For participant B, test–retest variability on foam is large in older adults, so the GO thresholds on both foam conditions lie above baseline and GO is not reached. This is a deliberate safety trade-off: the rules prefer a retest to a false clearance.

docs.title: A worked session
docs.text: This page follows participant A, a younger adult, from a simulated landing to an overall GO. Every value below is the output of the application for the corresponding example.

docs.title: 1 · Six hours after landing
docs.text:
Select A · younger adult · 6 h after landing.

Result six hours after a simulated landing.

The result is NO-GO under rule 3: on foam with eyes closed, the score is 40% of the participant's own baseline, below the 75% line. The other three conditions are at 80–96% of baseline but below the healthy population floor, which limits each of them to CAUTION under rule 4. The least favourable condition sets the overall result.

The recommended action reads: Do not leave the vehicle unassisted. Retest in approximately 63 h (≈69 h after landing). A retest, not this estimate, decides GO.

On the chart, each diamond is the participant's score, the solid green line is the GO threshold of that condition, the dotted brown line is the healthy population floor, and the open blue circle is the typical ISS crew member at the same time after landing (Wood et al. 2015, Table III).

docs.title: 2 · When to retest
docs.text:
Estimated retest time. The blue curve is the typical recovery rate applied to the measured deficit, the dashed line is the GO threshold and the shaded band is the range.

Foam with eyes closed determines the present NO-GO, but it recovers fastest (time constant 19.4 h). Firm floor with eyes open has a small deficit and a long time constant (116.1 h), and its GO threshold lies close to baseline, so it reaches its threshold last and sets the estimate: approximately 63 h after this session, with a range of 25–110 h derived from the published 95% confidence limits of the recovery time constant. The method is described in Retest estimate.

docs.title: 3 · First GO session, 69 h after landing
docs.text:
Select A · younger adult · 69 h after landing, first GO.

Every condition is GO, and the overall result remains CAUTION until a confirmatory session.

Every condition now reaches its GO threshold, so the session is GO. The overall result is CAUTION under rule 7, which requires two consecutive GO sessions at least 2 h apart. The card states: A confirmatory test is required in a separate session at least 2 h later (from 71 h after landing).

To continue in the application, press Record this session. The time advances to 71 h, and the next session counts only once its own scores have been entered.

docs.title: 4 · Confirmatory session, 71 h after landing
docs.text:
Select A · younger adult · 71 h after landing, confirmatory session, which contains both recorded sessions.

Two recorded GO sessions, 69 h and 71 h after landing.

The result is GO: No further testing is required under the decision rules. The egress decision rests with the crew surgeon. The session list shows both sessions and their source.

docs.title: 5 · Comparison with typical NASA crew
docs.text:
Each panel shows the NASA recovery curve of one condition, the participant's sessions and the GO threshold. The line below gives the difference from the typical crew member at the latest session.

With several recorded sessions, the points show whether the crew member is recovering faster or slower than the typical ISS crew member. Simulated sessions follow the typical curve by construction. The comparison is descriptive and does not enter the decision.

docs.title: Two further cases
docs.text:
A fall. In A · younger adult · baseline day, simulated fall, one trial on foam with eyes closed ends in a fall. The result is NO-GO under rule 2, whatever the score, and the card recommends referral to the crew surgeon and a repeat test in a separate session.

A fall gives NO-GO. The cross on the chart marks the condition in which it occurred.

No retest estimate. For participant C, whose baselines on the firm floor with eyes closed and on foam with eyes closed lie below the healthy population floor, the GO threshold cannot be reached under the recovery model. The card states that no retest time can be estimated and refers the crew member to the crew surgeon. The application does not extrapolate a time it cannot support.

Participant C six hours after a simulated landing.
